planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring into humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil; give it light shade and steady moisture the first season to help clumps establish before summer dry spells.

directions: Long-beaked sedge forms a graceful, weeping tussock of thin bright-green blades that arch outward like a fountain, distinguishing it from stiffer-textured woodland sedges. In early summer it sends up wiry stalks tipped with distinctive drooping seed heads whose long, curved beaks give the species its common name and add fine textural interest through fall. It tolerates more sun than many native sedges if soil stays evenly moist, but performs best in dappled shade under deciduous trees where it slowly increases into a non-aggressive clump. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges to keep the planting tidy.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown divisions in spring into consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in deep shade; avoid disturbing the shallow, slow-spreading roots once established, since this species resents transplanting after its first year.

directions: Fraser's sedge is an unmistakable Appalachian endemic that looks nothing like a typical sedge: it forms a low rosette of broad, glossy, strap-shaped evergreen leaves closer in appearance to galax or a small hosta, and in spring sends up short stalks topped with a single dense white ball of flowers. It is the sole species in its genus and a signature plant of rich, cove-forest understories, growing best in constantly moist, acidic soil with heavy leaf litter and deep shade. Because it spreads very slowly by rhizomes and resents root disturbance, it is best left undisturbed once sited, making it a long-term specimen for a shaded native woodland garden rather than a quick-filling groundcover.

planting.note: Set out divisions in spring in rich, moist woodland soil under full canopy shade; established plants tolerate summer dry spells better than many wide-leaved woodland sedges once their root systems mature.

directions: Carey's sedge produces unusually wide, soft, arching dark-green leaves that splay outward from the base in a loose rosette, giving it a coarser, more dramatic texture than fine-bladed woodland sedges like C. pensylvanica. It thrives in the deep, dry-to-moist shade of mature deciduous forests, spreading gradually by short rhizomes into slowly widening clumps rather than running aggressively. Its wide-leaved habit makes it a good textural companion to ferns and wildflowers in a shaded native planting, and it needs only a yearly cleanup of old foliage in late winter. It remains uncommon in the trade but is increasingly offered by specialty native plant nurseries.

planting.note: Plant plugs 10-14 inches apart in spring into moist to seasonally wet, humus-rich soil in shade to part shade; it colonizes readily by rhizomes to form a dense mat, so give it room to knit together as a lawn substitute.

directions: Low woodland sedge is a fine, low-mounding species that spreads steadily by rhizomes to form a soft, mowable-if-needed turf substitute in shaded areas where grass struggles, especially in the moist floodplain woods and bottomland soils it favors in the wild. Its short stature and colonizing habit make it one of the better native sedges for filling in as a walkable groundcover beneath trees, tolerating occasional foot traffic and light mowing far better than clump-forming woodland sedges. Give it consistent moisture through its first growing season; established plantings handle brief dry spells and seasonal wet soil equally well.

planting.note: Set plugs in spring into average, well-drained soil in part shade; this adaptable sedge tolerates a wider moisture range than most woodland species, from dry shade to moderately moist sites.

directions: Oval-leaf sedge forms neat, fine-textured tussocks topped by a distinctive tight, rounded cluster of flower spikes at the stem tip, unlike the more spread-out seed heads of many relatives. It is one of the more adaptable native woodland sedges, handling everything from dry, root-filled shade to average garden soil without fuss, which makes it a reliable filler between shrubs and perennials in a naturalistic shade border. Clumps increase slowly and stay well-behaved, so it pairs well with spreading groundcover sedges without being overwhelmed. Light shearing of old foliage in late winter keeps plantings looking fresh for spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into rich, consistently moist soil in dappled to full shade, such as a floodplain woodland or the moist edge of a rain garden bed.

directions: Davis' sedge is a wide-leaved woodland species best known for its distinctive bristly, awned seed heads that give summer flower spikes a shaggy, fringed look quite different from smoother-fruited sedges. It naturally inhabits moist bottomland forests and floodplain edges, so it is a good choice for a shaded rain garden or the damp margins of a woodland planting where soil stays reliably moist. Clumps form slowly and are non-aggressive, combining well with ferns, sedges, and spring ephemerals in a naturalistic wet-shade design. Established plants need little care beyond an annual tidy of old foliage.
